unsure.note: 7:133 jarād is a literal plague sent on Fir'awn's people while 54:7 is a simile for the dead emerging like scattering locusts — the shared material is only the insect; an intentional inversion (plague-creature onto resurrected deniers in a surah that retells Fir'awn's punishment) is possible but unproven.

The only two kursī in the Quran do invite a contrast — 2:255's Kursi encompassing the heavens and earth whose keeping never tires Him vs 38:34's royal kursī onto which a lifeless body is cast — but kursī is the ordinary word for a seat, neither passage gestures at the other, and the absolute-vs-emptied-sovereignty reading is a constructed contrast rather than demonstrable design.

Same lemma yanbūʿ in both, but 17:90 is the mockers' demanded miracle-spring and 39:21 is Allah threading rain into springs as a creation-sign; the irony that they demand what already flows around them is attractive, yet neither tadabbur nor classical tafsir ties these two verses, so the design claim is not earned.

Both are Form VIII of the rare plunge-verb — 90:11 the ascent of virtue not stormed, 38:59 a crowd storming into the Fire — and the inversion (the plunge refused in dunya vs. the plunge made into Hell) is well-formed, but neither tadabbur nor classical tafsir draws this pairing, so the antithesis remains my construction rather than evidenced design.

3:119 is the idiom of biting fingertips (anāmil) in suppressed rage at the believers, 25:27 the idiom of biting one's hands in Judgment-Day remorse — two distinct established Arabic gesture-idioms that happen to share the verb ʿaḍḍa; the rage-now/regret-later escalation reading is attractive but not anchored in either passage or the classical treatment.

41:11 dukhān is the primordial state of the proto-heaven at creation while 44:10 is a punishment smoke (on the dominant Ibn Masʿūd reading, the famine haze over Quraysh, not a cosmic state) — the tempting creation-to-eschaton bookend only holds under one side of a genuine tafsir ikhtilaf, so the designed connection is not earned.

Same rare verb of diminishing in both — 11:44 the flood water غِيضَ subsides at divine command, 13:8 the wombs تَغِيضُ fall short within divine measure — but the domains (flood resolution vs. embryology of divine knowledge) are unrelated and no tafsir warrant ties them; the shared root reads as ordinary vocabulary.

دهر occurs only twice (45:24 deniers' creed 'nothing destroys us but al-dahr'; 76:1 the span of dahr when man was nothing mentioned) and an elegant dialectic can be constructed — time deified as destroyer versus time as the mere container of man's non-existence — but the two uses diverge in construction and register and neither passage signals the other; the resonance is a reviewer's synthesis rather than earned surface material.

Two idiomatic uses of 'adud (arm-as-support) in unrelated contexts — 18:51 Allah 'would not take the misleaders as support' and 28:35 'We will strengthen your arm through your brother'; a theological contrast (He needs no helper yet grants one) can be constructed, but nothing in the surface material signals cross-reference, so the resonance is reviewer synthesis.

The vow-formula lā/lan abraḥ + ḥattā occurs only in these three places and twice inside Musa material (18:60 noble persistence toward the junction, 20:91 obstinate devotion to the calf until Musa returns), which tempts a designed contrast — but the shared material is a stock Arabic resolve-idiom applied to three unrelated situations (including Yusuf's brother in 12:80), and the resonance is not earned beyond the idiom itself.

5:12's نقيب (appointed tribal leader) is an unrelated sense; 18:97 (Ya'juj could not pierce the wall, نَقْبًا) and 50:36 (mighty generations نَقَّبُوا۟ bored through the lands yet found no escape) share the literal boring-through sense and a suggestive power-vs-futility mirror, but I cannot ground a designed connection beyond the shared root.

27:72 (the hastened doom already 'radifa lakum' — mounted behind the mockers) and 79:7 (ar-rādifah riding the first blast's back) both exploit the pillion-rider image in eschatological warning, but the image is the root's ordinary lexical content and its application differs (doom-behind-denier vs blast-behind-blast), while 8:9's murdifīn (angels in succession) has the opposite valence — the alignment is suggestive but not clearly designed.

The root's shared sense 'beyond the obligatory' is its ordinary lexical content: anfāl as spoils (8:1), nāfilah as the Prophet's extra devotion (17:79), and nāfilah as Yaʿqūb the unasked-for extra gift (21:72) — the mirrored surplus (servant's extra worship / Lord's extra gift) between 17:79 and 21:72 is suggestive but rests on no shared scene, phrase, or argument.

The two Form-IV uses (70:18 'جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ' hoarding wealth; 84:23 'بِمَا يُوعُونَ' harboring denial) share a container metaphor for the damned's hidden accumulation, but the objects and registers differ enough that designed echo versus ordinary containment idiom cannot be settled — and 12:76 (saddlebags) and 69:12 (the retaining ear) show the root is common container vocabulary.

The root splits into two unrelated lexemes — dhimmah 'treaty-bond' (9:8, 9:10) and madhmūm 'blamed' (17:18, 17:22, 68:49); the madhmūman refrain is an intra-Isra device (مذموما مدحورا / مذموما مخذولا), and extending it to Yunus's averted disgrace ('لنُبذ بالعراء وهو مذموم' 68:49) rests on the bare adjective rather than a demonstrable designed pairing.

The only two sunbulah passages (2:261 'seven sanābil, each with a hundred grains' and 12:43-49 'seven green sunbulāt... leave it in its sunbul') share the striking seven-plus-grain-ears collocation, but the themes never touch (charity multiplication vs famine storage), neither tadabbur nor classical tafsir draws the link, and seven ears is natural agrarian imagery — I cannot earn the design claim.
